title: Most models miss SNAP's minimum benefit when broad-based categorical eligibility lifts the income limits
paragraphs: For each of {householdCount} households that qualify for SNAP food benefits, most of the {nModels} models on PolicyBench answer $0. SNAP pays every eligible household of one or two people at least a minimum benefit, so a $0 answer calls the household ineligible and could keep someone who qualifies from applying. PolicyEngine puts the correct amount for each household at that minimum, ${minimumMonthly} a month or ${referenceAmount} for 2026. Of the {answers} answers PolicyBench requests for these households, {zeroAnswers} come to $0 and {hits} match the correct amount.

Each household qualifies only through broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE). Under BBCE, a state extends SNAP to households that receive, or are authorized to receive, a non-cash benefit funded by Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF). Connecticut, Michigan, and Wisconsin open that benefit to households with gross income up to {bbceGrossLimitHigh}% of the federal poverty guideline, and Texas up to {bbceGrossLimitTx}%, against SNAP's ordinary limit of {snapGrossLimit}%. None of these states applies a net income test to the benefit, and only Texas keeps an asset limit.

All {householdCount} households have gross income above {snapGrossLimit}% of the guideline. A Michigan worker who pays child support and a {txAge}-year-old Texas resident with wages and ${financialAssistance} of financial assistance fail SNAP's ordinary gross income test. A Connecticut couple on Social Security disability income, a disabled Michigan resident living alone, and an {wiAge}-year-old surviving spouse in Wisconsin fail SNAP's ordinary net income test. All three have an elderly or disabled member, and SNAP exempts such households from the gross income test. The Connecticut couple also holds ${ctSavings} in savings, above SNAP's asset limit. Each household has one or two people and falls under its state's BBCE limit, and at these incomes SNAP's ordinary formula pays nothing, so each gets the minimum.

When savings rather than income stand in the way, most models answer above $0. PolicyBench also asks models about households in New Jersey, North Carolina, Virginia, and Pennsylvania that pass SNAP's income tests but hold savings above its asset limit, which BBCE removes in those states. For those {assetOnlyCount} households, {assetOnlyAbove0Share}% of answers come in above $0, against {fiveAbove0Share}% for the {householdCount} held back by income. GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Fable 5.1 answer above $0 for each household held back by savings and $0 for each of the {householdCount} held back by income.

PolicyBench asks each model to explain every answer. For the households held back by savings, {assetOnlyBbceMentions} of {assetOnlyExplanations} explanations mention BBCE, by name or as categorical eligibility, and {assetOnlyBbceAssets} of those also mention assets. For the {householdCount} held back by income, {fiveBbceMentions} of {explanations} explanations mention BBCE, and {fiveBbceZeros} of those still end at $0. Of those {fiveBbceZeros}, {fiveBbceZeroWithNetLimit} mention a net income limit or test, though none of these households' states applies one under BBCE.

GPT-6 Astra gets {astraHits} of the {householdCount} households right, more than any other model, and cites the state's BBCE limit of {bbceGrossLimitHigh}% of the guideline each time. It answers $0 for the Texas resident and the Michigan worker, the two households that fail SNAP's ordinary gross income test. Claude Opus 5.5 answers ${opusOn108} for the Wisconsin surviving spouse, citing Wisconsin's BBCE and its {bbceGrossLimitHigh}% limit. For the Connecticut couple and the disabled Michigan resident it answers $0, citing SNAP's ordinary net income test, which BBCE removes in both states. GPT-6 Sol, which leads PolicyBench overall, answers $0 for {sol6ZeroCount} of the {householdCount} and mentions BBCE in {sol6BbceMentions} of its {boardHouseholds} SNAP explanations.

For the Texas resident, GPT-6 Sol answers ${sol6On030} and Claude Opus 5.5 answers ${opusOn030}, and both compute an ordinary benefit from wages alone. PolicyEngine also counts the ${financialAssistance} of financial assistance as income, which puts the household above SNAP's ordinary limits and leaves BBCE as its only route. The prompt labels that money only "financial assistance", so both answers turn on what counts as income, not on BBCE.

Prompts mention TANF only to ask for the household's TANF amount, and none mentions the non-cash benefit. Every prompt tells the model to treat any unlisted household fact or status "as false", to assume "program take-up when required", and not to infer unlisted "benefit receipt". PolicyEngine applies BBCE to any household eligible for the non-cash benefit, without checking whether the household receives it or is authorized to receive it. A model that requires receipt or authorization falls back on SNAP's ordinary tests, and each of the {householdCount} fails at least one. Of the {zeroAnswers} $0 answers, {zeroTanfMentions} mentions TANF: Claude Sonnet 4.6 writes that the Texas resident receives neither TANF nor SSI.

The September 3 note counted {previousHouseholdCount} households at ${previousReference} each; PolicyBench now scores {householdCount} of them, at ${referenceAmount}. The ${previousReference} came from the correct amounts PolicyBench froze on July 3, which used an unrounded minimum: ${previousMonthlyJanSep} a month through September and a projected ${previousMonthlyOctDec} from October. PolicyEngine began rounding the minimum to the nearest dollar on July 28 (policyengine-us #9162), and PolicyBench's September 22 amounts apply that fix. PolicyBench no longer scores the other household, in Texas, because PolicyEngine computed its amount with {assumedHours} hours of work a week, which the prompt does not list. Under the prompt's rule that unlisted numbers are 0, the time limit for able-bodied adults without dependents applies, and PolicyEngine gives $0, the same answer as the top three models in that note. That note also said these states waive the asset test, but Texas keeps a ${bbceAssetLimitTx} asset limit.
